title: Stop look-alike handles at sign-up

blocks.text: Members of a community site choose a public handle at sign-up. Last week someone registered `ｓｕｐｐｏｒｔ`, in full-width letters. On a profile page it looks like the staff account, and the mention service, which looks handles up after NFKC normalisation, now delivers some `@support` mentions to it. A second account, `ѕupport`, starts with a Cyrillic letter.
`HandleRegistry.register` already refuses reserved and taken handles. Finish the two `TODO`s in `src/main/java/practice/HandleRegistry.java`:

items: `canonical(raw)`: the form of the handle that the registry checks, stores and compares;
`allowed(handle)`: whether the handle keeps to the rules below.

blocks.text: A handle is 3 to 20 characters long, each one a lowercase letter of the Latin script (accents are fine: `zoë_m`, `renée`), a digit `0`–`9`, or `_`. When you're done, any two spellings the mention service treats as one handle are one handle here too, and a handle that only looks like a Latin one is refused. About three lines in total.

cases.says: handles made of lowercase Latin letters (accents included), digits and underscores register and come back as typed
handles shorter than three characters are refused
a reserved handle and a handle someone already has are refused
a reserved handle typed in full-width letters is refused
a handle typed in full-width characters counts as the handle it spells, so it is taken if that one is
a handle with a Cyrillic or Greek letter that looks Latin is refused
a handle is refused when only part of it keeps to the rules: a dot, a space, a capital or too many characters

origin.section: Validate the Value the Next Layer Will Use, Against an Allow-List

concepts: Input is decoded and normalised the way the next layer will, then the whole canonical string is matched against an allow-list, and the canonical value is passed on.
NFKC folds full-width forms into ASCII but leaves look-alike letters of other scripts unchanged; only the allow-list's character range refuses them.
